newsitem.title: ZAIRE: ZAIRE'S KABILA CLAIMS VICTORY, MOBUTU IN MOROCCO. [CORRECTED 09:36 GMT]
newsitem.headline: ZAIRE'S KABILA CLAIMS VICTORY, MOBUTU IN MOROCCO. [CORRECTED 09:36 GMT]

text.p: Laurent Kabila and his rebels have proclaimed victory in Zaire's seven-month civil war and ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko has fled to Morocco.

Kabila, 56, declared himself head of state in a statement he read at his headquarters in the southern mining city of Lubumbashi on Saturday as his forces moved into the capital Kinshasa virtually unopposed, to the cheers of residents.
He purged Africa's third largest nation of one of the more obvious symbols of Mobutu's rule -- its name.
"Mr Laurent Desire Kabila assumes from today the functions of the head of state of the Democratic Republic of the Congo," the statement said.
This was the name Zaire had from 1964 until Mobutu changed it in 1971 (corrects from "...the name Zaire had on independence from Belgium in 1960 until Mobutu changed it in 1971").

Sporadic exchanges of mortar and automatic weapons fire were heard at nightfall in Kinshasa and reports of shootouts with diehard Mobutu loyalists suggested the rebels still had to consolidate their hold over the city of five million people.

In its first broadcast over national radio in Kinshasa, the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire ordered all government troops to report by Sunday morning and warned looters they would be severely punished.
Mobutu and his family flew to the Moroccan capital Rabat aboard three Gabonese aircraft late on Saturday night, a senior Moroccan security official said on Sunday.
He had fled from Kinshasa on Friday and was reported to have gone to his jungle palace at his northern ancestral home of Gbadolite.

"Mobutu and his family arrived aboard three airplanes discreetly in the Rabat military airport. Mobutu and his family will stay at the 50-room Amphitrite Hotel," the official told Reuters. The hotel is some 20 km (12 miles) south of Rabat on the Atlantic coast close to the royal palace of Skhirat.
"Three Gabonese aircraft transported Mobutu and his family to the Rabat military airport thanks to the cooperation of Moroccan authorities," said the official.
He could not say how long the former leader would be staying in Morocco. "Mobutu and his family are expected to move later to the southern city of Marrakesh," the official said.
He declined to give any further details but a reliable source told Reuters that work had been under way at a luxury villa in Marrakesh in preparation for Mobutu.
A Reuters correspondent saw an unusual deployment of security forces around the Amphitrite hotel.
"The hotel was booked for Mobutu and his family...Therefore it is now not open to the public," said a Moroccan official.

Mobutu met Morocco's King Hassan in February when he stopped in Rabat on his way home to Zaire from Europe. Kabila, whose revolt mushroomed from an October dispute over Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis, said he would set up a transitional government of public salvation within 72 hours.

He also pledged a constituent assembly within 60 days to work out a transitional constitution to replace the one agreed after a reluctant Mobutu bowed to foreign and domestic pressure for multi-party politics in 1990.
The United States, former colonial power Belgium, France, one of Mobutu's last friends, and Germany reacted to Kabila's victory by calling for a broad-based government and elections.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, speaking in Moscow, had a similar message for Kabila, urging him to respect the "choice and the voice" of the Zairean people.
Mobutu, 66 and suffering from cancer, seized power in 1965 and proved one of Africa's most enduring strongmen. Western powers supported him as a Cold War bastion against Soviet communism.

Critics denounced him as everything from a dictator to a thief and accused him of plundering what is potentially one of Africa's richest countries and amassing a huge personal fortune while his people struggled against poverty and neglect.
Mobutu refused to resign as head of state, as demanded by Kabila, but his abrupt departure from the capital on Friday triggered intense speculation that he was on his way to exile.

Initial reports on casualties in Kinshasa as the rebels moved in were sketchy, but defence minister and army chief of staff General Mahele Lieko Bokungo was killed on Friday night by members of the presidential guard.
Diplomats said Mahele had been planning to meet Kabila to discuss handing over power.
The United States welcomed what it called a relatively smooth transfer of power and urged the new leadership to establish an inclusive transitional government leading to elections.
